LONDON, England (CNN) -- The designers behind a "thinking" yacht are hoping to break a world record by sending it across the Atlantic Ocean without any human assistance. The autonomous yacht Avalon is hoisted to have her keel put in place before launching . The four-meter boat, "Avalon", was designed and built by an eight-strong team of third-year engineering students at Swiss science university ETH Zurich. The students are planning to take the boat to a robotic sailing regatta in July, before launching it into the Microtransat Transatlantic challenge in early September. Using sensors to detect the speed and direction of the wind, the boat is programmed to reach a given co-ordinate and will attain it by automatically adapting to the changing conditions. One of the "Students Sailing Autonomously" (SSA) team's project managers, Hendrik Erckens, told CNN that if the Atlantic crossing succeeds it will be a world record as an unmanned boat has not previously made the voyage. It is planned the crossing will begin from the west coast of Ireland and finish in the Caribbean. "For us the Microtransat challenge is the big goal. I'm pretty confident we can do it. This week in testing it is pretty much doing what it's supposed to do. And it is water tight. "Over the last couple of days we tried some autonomous tacks and jibes and now we are testing the navigation," he said. See photos of the autonomous yacht from construction to launch » . The team has been working on the project since September 2008, and are currently at the on-water testing stage, having designed and built the boat. While the team will be able to track the boat through an onboard global positioning system (GPS) during the transatlantic voyage, Erckens said as long as the challenge is active they won't have any control over the vessel. "We will set it out and it will be completely autonomous. There are solar cells on the back for power and extra power supplies on board. "There is a satellite communication system on board and the boat can download weather information by itself so it can calculate the best route to travel," he said. Erckens said the team is positive that the carbon-fibre boat will survive the rough Atlantic seas -- an issue that has stopped many manned crossings before -- including Richard Branson's attempt at the fastest transatlantic crossing aboard the 99-foot Virgin Money last fall. "We feel our advantage over other teams is that we are mechanical engineers. We have designed this boat ourselves and exactly for this purpose." Erckens said the idea could one day offer a new autopilot option for large yachts. "The idea came as there are autopilots for boats out there, but currently the commercially available autopilots only steer the rudder. We are looking to control the sails as well."

LONDON, England (CNN) -- A team that created a "thinking" yacht is aiming to set a world record by sending their vessel across the Atlantic without any people on board to guide it.

Named "Avalon," the four-meter craft was conceived and constructed by a group of eight engineering students in their third year at ETH Zurich, a science-focused university in Switzerland. Their plan involves entering the vessel in a robotic sailing competition during July, and then submitting it to the Microtransat Transatlantic challenge at the start of September.

The yacht relies on sensors that measure both wind speed and direction, allowing it to be programmed toward a specific coordinate, which it reaches by automatically adjusting to whatever conditions it encounters. Hendrik Erckens, one of the project managers within the "Students Sailing Autonomously" (SSA) team, explained to CNN that a successful Atlantic voyage would establish a world record, since no crewless boat has ever completed such a journey before. The route is set to depart from Ireland's western coastline and conclude in the Caribbean.

"The Microtransat challenge represents our main objective. I feel fairly certain we can accomplish it. During this week's tests, it's basically performing as intended. And it doesn't leak," he said. "In recent days we've attempted several autonomous tacks and jibes, and at this point we're evaluating the navigation."

The group has devoted themselves to this endeavor since September 2008, and after finishing the design and construction, they have reached the phase of testing on the water. Although an onboard GPS system will let the team monitor the boat throughout its Atlantic passage, Erckens noted that they will have zero authority over the vessel while the challenge remains underway.

"Once we release it, it will function entirely on its own. Solar panels are mounted at the rear to generate energy, and additional power sources are carried on board as well," he said. "It also has a satellite communication system, and the boat is able to retrieve weather data independently, enabling it to work out the ideal route."

According to Erckens, the team is confident their carbon-fibre boat can endure the harsh Atlantic waters -- a challenge that has defeated numerous crewed crossings, among them Richard Branson's bid last fall to achieve the quickest transatlantic passage aboard the 99-foot Virgin Money.

"What gives us an edge over rival teams is that we're mechanical engineers. We built this boat with our own hands, specifically for this task."

Erckens suggested the concept might eventually provide a fresh autopilot alternative for sizable yachts. "The concept emerged because boat autopilots already exist, but the ones you can buy today only manage the rudder. Our aim is to govern the sails too."

A team of engineering students at ETH Zurich, one of Switzerland's leading technical universities, has undertaken an ambitious project that pushes the boundaries of autonomous marine navigation. These sensors continuously detect both wind speed and wind direction, providing the yacht with the critical data it needs to make real-time sailing decisions. Rather than following a rigid, pre-programmed path, Avalon is designed to navigate toward a series of set coordinates while automatically adapting to the ever-changing conditions of the sea. This means the yacht can adjust its course and sail configuration on the fly, responding intelligently to shifting winds and weather much as an experienced human sailor would.

## The Microtransat Challenge

Avalon was built to compete in the Microtransat challenge, a demanding competition that tests the limits of autonomous sailing technology. The challenge calls for an unmanned boat to complete a transatlantic crossing, sailing all the way from Ireland to the Caribbean. This route spans thousands of kilometers of unpredictable open ocean, presenting an extraordinary test of both the vessel's engineering and its autonomous decision-making systems.

The stakes for Avalon are historic. Should the yacht successfully complete its unmanned transatlantic voyage, it would set a new world record, as no unmanned boat has ever managed to make this crossing before. # Student-Built Autonomous Yacht 'Avalon' Sets Sail on Record-Breaking Atlantic Crossing

*By CNN Staff*

**ZURICH, Switzerland** — A team of engineering students from ETH Zurich has launched an ambitious bid to make history, sending an unmanned autonomous sailboat named "Avalon" across the Atlantic Ocean in an attempt to set a world record for autonomous ocean crossing.

The vessel, which its creators describe as a "thinking" yacht, departed with no crew aboard, relying entirely on sophisticated onboard computers, sensors, and artificial intelligence to navigate thousands of miles of open ocean.

## A Robot at the Helm

Unlike traditional sailboats, Avalon makes its own decisions. The 4-meter-long autonomous vessel continuously analyzes wind conditions, wave patterns, and its position using GPS and a suite of onboard sensors. Its control system adjusts the sails and rudder in real time, charting an efficient course toward its destination without any human intervention.

"The boat has to think for itself out there," said one team member. "There's no one to make corrections. Every decision — how to handle a sudden gust, how to avoid an obstacle, how to conserve energy — has to be made by the system alone."

Power for the electronics comes from solar panels, allowing the boat to sustain its computing systems throughout the weeks-long journey.

## Engineering Against the Odds

The Atlantic represents a formidable challenge for an autonomous craft. The team must contend with unpredictable storms, powerful currents, mechanical wear, and the ever-present risk of collisions with ships or debris. Reliability is paramount, as any failure hundreds of miles from shore could end the mission instantly.

The students designed Avalon to be rugged and self-sufficient, capable of weathering harsh conditions while maintaining a steady course. Communication with the team on shore is maintained via satellite, allowing engineers to monitor the vessel's progress and health — though they cannot steer it themselves.

## Pushing the Boundaries of Autonomy

The project reflects a growing global interest in autonomous marine technology, which holds promise for applications ranging from oceanographic research and environmental monitoring to unmanned cargo transport.

For the ETH Zurich students, the crossing is both an academic milestone and a test of their engineering ambitions. Success would place their names in the record books and demonstrate the viability of small, intelligent autonomous vessels for long-distance ocean voyages.

As Avalon presses forward through the swells of the Atlantic, its team watches anxiously from Switzerland, hoping their creation can prove that a robotic sailor can conquer one of the world's most demanding oceans — entirely on its own.

---

# Swiss Engineering Students Set Sail with Autonomous Robotic Boat for Transatlantic Challenge

**ZURICH** — A team of engineering students from Switzerland has unveiled an autonomous robotic sailboat designed to cross the Atlantic Ocean without any human intervention, joining an elite group of competitors in the notoriously difficult Microtransat Challenge.

The vessel, a sleek 2.4-meter craft named *Helvetia*, represents more than two years of design, testing, and refinement by a multidisciplinary team of students specializing in mechanical engineering, robotics, and computer science.

"What started as an ambitious classroom project has become something we truly believe can make history," said Lena Furrer, the project's manager. "We wanted to prove that a small student team, working with limited resources, could build a machine capable of surviving one of the harshest environments on the planet."

## A Test of Endurance and Engineering

The Microtransat Challenge, launched in 2010, invites teams worldwide to build fully autonomous boats capable of crossing the Atlantic Ocean. To complete the roughly 3,000-kilometer voyage, vessels must navigate storms, powerful currents, and weeks of isolation while relying entirely on onboard systems for propulsion, navigation, and decision-making.

The challenge has proven remarkably unforgiving. Since its inception, only a handful of boats have successfully completed the crossing, with most falling victim to equipment failure, collisions with ships, or the relentless pounding of ocean waves.

"The statistics are humbling," Furrer admitted. "The Atlantic doesn't care how clever your code is. We've designed *Helvetia* to be robust above all else—if a system fails, the boat needs to recover on its own and keep going."

## Solar Power and Smart Navigation

*Helvetia* is powered entirely by wind for propulsion and solar panels for its electronics, allowing it to operate indefinitely without refueling. The team equipped the boat with a suite of sensors, GPS units, and a custom-built navigation algorithm that adjusts the sail and rudder in real time based on weather conditions.

A satellite communication system will allow the team to monitor the boat's progress from Switzerland, though they will be unable to control it directly once it enters competition mode.

"The most challenging part wasn't building the hardware—it was teaching the boat to think," said one of the team's software engineers. "It has to make thousands of small decisions every day, balancing speed against safety, all while conserving energy."

## Looking Ahead

The team plans to launch *Helvetia* from the coast of France later this year, sending it on a westward journey toward the Caribbean. If successful, the crossing could take anywhere from three to six months.

"Win or lose, we've already learned more than we ever imagined," Furrer said. "But of course, we'd love to see our little boat reach the other side. That would be the ultimate reward for all these late nights."

For now, the students continue their final rounds of testing on Swiss lakes, preparing their creation for the vast and unpredictable ocean that awaits.

# The Ghost Ship That Sails Itself: How an Unmanned Vessel Conquered the Atlantic

*By CNN Staff*

---

Somewhere in the vast expanse of the North Atlantic, a sleek vessel cuts through churning gray waters, its sails trimmed perfectly to catch the wind. There is no captain at the helm. No crew scrambling across the deck. No human hand anywhere aboard.

Yet the ship knows exactly where it is going.

This is the *Meridian*, a 23-foot autonomous sailing vessel that has spent the past 42 days crossing one of the world's most treacherous oceans entirely on its own—guided by satellites, informed by sensors, and steered by algorithms that make thousands of decisions every hour without a single word from shore.

"What we're witnessing is nothing short of a revolution in maritime navigation," said Dr. Elena Marsh, a robotics engineer who has followed the vessel's progress from a control center in Plymouth, England. "For centuries, crossing the Atlantic meant risking human lives. Now we're proving that machines can do it alone."

## A Journey Without a Soul Aboard

The *Meridian* departed from the coast of Newfoundland in early autumn, pointing its bow toward the coast of Ireland some 2,000 nautical miles away. Its mission: to complete an unassisted transatlantic crossing while gathering critical oceanographic data along the way.

At its heart, the vessel relies on three interlocking technologies. GPS provides its precise position on the globe, accurate to within a few meters. An array of sensors—measuring wind speed, wave height, barometric pressure, and hull orientation—feeds a constant stream of information to the onboard computer. And a satellite communication link allows the vessel to transmit its status back to engineers and receive occasional software updates.

"The boat is essentially thinking for itself," explained Marcus Chen, lead systems architect on the project. "Every few seconds, it's asking: Where am I? Where is the wind coming from? What obstacles are ahead? And then it adjusts."

Unlike motorized drones that burn through fuel, the *Meridian* harnesses only the wind for propulsion and solar panels for its electronics. This makes it capable of theoretically indefinite voyages—a quality that has caught the attention of scientists and militaries alike.

## The Challenge of the Open Sea

The Atlantic does not forgive.

During its crossing, the *Meridian* endured two major storms, including one that generated waves exceeding 20 feet. Wind gusts approached 50 knots. For a vessel with no human aboard to reef the sails or hold the wheel, these were the ultimate tests.

"There was a moment during the second storm when we lost contact for nearly six hours," Chen recalled, his voice tightening at the memory. "We had no idea if the boat had capsized or been dismasted. When the signal came back, and we saw it had righted itself and stayed on course—that was the moment we knew we had built something remarkable."

The vessel's self-correcting keel and weighted hull are designed to recover from knockdowns, while its collision-avoidance system uses radar and automatic identification signals to detect and steer clear of cargo ships, fishing boats, and even drifting debris.

## Eyes on the Ocean

Beyond the engineering triumph, the *Meridian* carries a scientific purpose. As it sailed, its instruments continuously sampled sea surface temperatures, salinity levels, and microplastic concentrations—data that is notoriously expensive and difficult to collect across such a vast area.

"A research vessel with a full crew can cost tens of thousands of dollars a day to operate," said Dr. Marsh. "A vessel like this can gather comparable data at a fraction of the cost, and it can go places we'd never risk sending people."

Climate scientists have expressed particular interest in the technology's potential to monitor the ocean's changing chemistry, offering a persistent presence in remote waters where traditional monitoring is sparse.

## Not Without Controversy

The rise of autonomous vessels has not been universally celebrated. Maritime unions have raised concerns about the future of seafaring jobs, while legal experts point to a murky regulatory landscape.

"Who is liable if an unmanned vessel collides with a fishing boat?" asked James Okoro, a maritime law specialist. "International law was written with human crews in mind. This technology is racing ahead of our ability to govern it."

There are security implications as well. Defense analysts note that the same technology enabling peaceful ocean research could be adapted for surveillance or military reconnaissance—a dual-use dilemma that few nations have fully addressed.

## The Horizon Ahead

As the *Meridian* approaches the Irish coast, its creators are already planning bolder missions: a Pacific crossing, polar expeditions, and eventually a fleet of vessels working in coordination to map the world's oceans.

"This is just the beginning," Chen said. "In ten years, I believe autonomous vessels will be as common as satellites are in orbit. The ocean is the last great frontier we've barely explored. These boats are how we'll finally understand it."

For now, the little vessel sails on—silent, tireless, and utterly alone—carrying with it a glimpse of a future where the machines have learned to master the sea.

---

*This story is part of CNN's ongoing coverage of emerging technologies reshaping our world.*

# Student-Built Autonomous Yacht Sets Sights on Transatlantic Crossing

**A four-meter carbon-fibre vessel, designed and constructed by university students, prepares to attempt an unmanned voyage from Ireland to the Caribbean**

---

In a workshop humming with the sound of grinding tools and the sharp scent of curing resin, a team of engineering and marine science students has spent the better part of two years building something they hope will make history: a fully autonomous sailing yacht capable of crossing the Atlantic Ocean without a single person aboard.

The vessel, measuring just four meters from bow to stern, is constructed almost entirely from carbon fibre—a material chosen for its exceptional strength-to-weight ratio. At a time when autonomous technology dominates headlines on land and in the air, this student project represents an ambitious foray into one of the most unforgiving testing grounds imaginable: the open sea.

## Engineering for the Elements

The design philosophy behind the yacht prioritizes resilience above all else. Once it leaves port, there will be no crew to make repairs, adjust the rigging, or bail out water. Every system must function independently for weeks at a time.

"The ocean doesn't care about your deadlines or your assumptions," said one team member during a recent testing session. "Everything has to be redundant. If one component fails, another has to take over."

The hull's carbon-fibre construction keeps the total weight low while maintaining the rigidity needed to withstand pounding waves and sustained structural stress. Solar panels mounted across the deck feed a bank of batteries, powering the onboard computer, navigation sensors, and the servo motors that control the rudder and sails.

At the heart of the vessel is its guidance system—a network of GPS receivers, wind sensors, and a compass feeding data to an onboard computer. Using this information, the yacht continuously calculates its position, adjusts its heading, and trims its sails to make the best possible progress toward a series of pre-programmed waypoints. A satellite communication link allows the team to monitor the boat's progress from shore and, if necessary, upload new instructions.

## Testing on Home Waters

Before committing their creation to the Atlantic, the students have subjected it to a rigorous testing regime in coastal waters. These trials serve to validate the boat's ability to hold a course, respond to shifting winds, and recover its intended heading after being knocked off track by waves or gusts.

Early tests revealed the kinds of problems that only real-world conditions expose: waterproofing weaknesses, software bugs that caused erratic steering, and questions about how the sails would perform under sustained load. Each failure fed back into the design, prompting revisions to both hardware and code.

Capsize recovery has been a particular focus. In heavy seas, a small vessel can be rolled by breaking waves, and the design must allow the boat to right itself and continue sailing. The team has also worked to ensure the yacht can shed water quickly and keep its sensitive electronics dry throughout the crossing.

## The Route Ahead

The planned voyage will begin off the coast of Ireland, with the yacht setting out into the North Atlantic before turning southwest toward the Caribbean. The route is designed to take advantage of prevailing winds and currents, following in the wake—loosely speaking—of the trade winds that have carried sailors across the ocean for centuries.

The journey is expected to cover thousands of kilometers and take weeks, possibly months, depending on weather. Along the way, the boat will contend with shipping lanes, storms, marine debris, and the ever-present risk of collision or entanglement. Even the growth of barnacles and algae on the hull could slow it enough to jeopardize the mission.

Should it complete the crossing, the vessel would join a small but growing group of autonomous craft to have traversed an ocean unaided—a feat that remains far from routine.

## Beyond the Record

For the students, the transatlantic attempt is about more than reaching a distant shoreline. The project has become a proving ground for skills that classroom instruction alone cannot provide: composite fabrication, embedded software, systems integration, and the discipline of designing for failure.

There is also a scientific dimension. Autonomous vessels like this one offer a low-cost platform for gathering oceanographic data—recording water temperature, wave conditions, and other measurements across vast stretches of sea that research ships rarely visit. The students envision their work contributing, however modestly, to a future in which fleets of small robotic craft help monitor the health of the world's oceans.

Whether or not the little carbon-fibre yacht reaches the Caribbean, its builders have already learned lessons that no textbook could deliver. And somewhere off the Irish coast, when the moorings are finally slipped and the boat turns its bow toward the open Atlantic, they will watch their creation sail beyond the horizon—alone.

# Student-Built Autonomous Sailboat Charts Its Own Course Using Onboard Weather Intelligence

*Engineering students unveil a self-sailing vessel that adjusts its own sails and pulls live weather data without human input*

---

A team of undergraduate engineering students has unveiled an autonomous sailboat capable of navigating open water, trimming its own sails, and downloading real-time weather data—all without a human hand on the tiller.

The project, which took roughly 18 months to develop, represents a growing trend of student-led robotics efforts tackling one of the more difficult challenges in autonomous systems: harnessing an unpredictable natural power source like wind.

## How the Boat Controls Its Sails

At the heart of the vessel is a control system that continuously adjusts the sails to match wind conditions—a task that traditionally requires an experienced sailor.

"The hardest part isn't steering, it's the sail control," explained Maya Chen, the team's lead controls engineer. "A motor turns the rudder, sure, but wind is chaotic. We use a wind vane sensor at the top of the mast that feeds data to our onboard computer several times per second. The system calculates the optimal sail angle for the current wind direction and speed, then a winch motor pulls the lines in or lets them out."

The boat relies on a combination of an anemometer, GPS, and an inertial measurement unit to understand its position and orientation.

"Think of it as a feedback loop," Chen said. "The computer knows where the boat is pointed, where it wants to go, and where the wind is coming from. It's constantly solving that equation and making small corrections. If a gust hits, the sail eases out automatically to keep us from heeling over too far."

The team wrote custom firmware that runs on a low-power microcontroller, chosen specifically to conserve battery during multi-day voyages.

## Downloading Its Own Weather Data

Perhaps the most ambitious feature is the boat's ability to retrieve weather forecasts on its own and use them to plan a route.

"We didn't want a boat that just reacts to the wind in front of it," said Diego Ramirez, the software team lead. "We wanted it to think ahead. So we built a system that connects over a satellite modem and pulls down GRIB files—those are compressed weather forecast files that sailors use for wind and current predictions."

Once the data arrives, an onboard routing algorithm gets to work.

"The algorithm looks at the forecast wind fields across a whole region and calculates the fastest safe path to the destination," Ramirez explained. "It's basically doing what a human navigator does with a chart and a coffee, except it recalculates every few hours as new forecasts come in. If a storm is developing along our planned route, the boat can reroute itself before it ever gets there."

Because bandwidth over satellite is expensive and slow, the team had to be clever about data usage.

"We compress everything and only download the specific geographic area we care about," Ramirez said. "A full global forecast would be enormous. We request a tight window around our position and heading, which keeps the file small and the download quick."

## Building on a Student Budget

The team emphasized that the project was built with off-the-shelf components and a modest budget, making the effort reproducible for other student groups.

"We're not working with a defense contractor's checkbook," said Priya Patel, the project's faculty-supervised team manager. "A lot of this is a repurposed hobby sailboat hull, some marine-grade electronics, and a lot of 3 a.m. debugging sessions. The point was to prove that a student team could pull this off."

Patel noted that reliability, not speed, was the real test.

"Anyone can make a robot boat work in a calm pond for ten minutes," she said. "The challenge is making it survive days at sea, handle wet electronics, keep its solar panels charged, and recover gracefully when something goes wrong. That's the engineering that actually matters."

## What Comes Next

The team plans to enter their vessel in an international autonomous sailing competition, where robotic boats attempt long-distance crossings with no human intervention.

"Our dream is an unmanned ocean crossing," Chen said. "These boats could one day gather ocean data—temperature, salinity, pollution—in places research vessels rarely go, and do it for a fraction of the cost."

For now, the students are focused on continued testing in local waters, refining the sail-control software one gust at a time.

"Every time it corrects itself without us touching anything," Ramirez said, "it still feels a little like magic."
